note: Maps the token cost of reasoning models and the methods that cut it, the cost side of any reasoning deployment case.
title: Efficient Inference for Large Reasoning Models: A Survey
journal: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence

reading.body:
Reasoning models achieve superior performance by working through problems step-by-step, but token costs during inference make them expensive to deploy at scale, and efficiency techniques that reduce this cost without sacrificing quality determine whether reasoning becomes practical.

Reasoning models produce better answers than standard systems because they generate explicit intermediate steps, but these steps consume tokens proportionally to their length. The efficiency gap matters for AI infrastructure because token consumption directly translates to compute requirements, power draw, and ultimately the data center capacity needed to serve reasoning workloads. As reasoning models become more capable, their inference costs grow faster than training costs, making deployment feasibility a function of how much the token footprint can be compressed.

Two distinct approaches address this cost problem. Explicit methods keep the reasoning steps visible and interpretable while making them more compact, preserving the ability to audit how the model reached its answer. Implicit methods encode reasoning in the model's hidden states rather than in token sequences, reducing output tokens but sacrificing interpretability. The choice between these approaches involves a tradeoff: visibility and control versus raw efficiency.

The survey does not quantify absolute cost reductions from these techniques or compare their performance across specific deployment scenarios. It does not establish which efficiency approach works best for which reasoning problems, or whether the gains in tokens per inference translate to meaningful power or infrastructure savings in production systems. What it does map is the landscape of available methods, which determines the ceiling for how cheap reasoning inference can become.

explain_beginner: AI models that reason step by step before answering give better answers, but that thinking process can use an enormous number of words internally, which costs real money and time before a single final answer appears. This survey catalogs the different ways researchers are trying to cut that cost without losing the quality benefit. It groups the approaches into two families, ones that keep the visible step by step reasoning but make it shorter and less repetitive, and ones that hide the reasoning entirely inside the model's internal calculations so it never has to be written out as text at all. The paper argues this efficiency question is not a side issue, it is what determines whether advanced reasoning AI becomes cheap enough for everyday products or stays too expensive for anything but special, high value use cases only.
explain_business: The direct cost lesson here is that a reasoning model's expense is not fixed, it is a design choice that can be tuned along a real tradeoff between token cost, latency, and answer quality, and this survey maps the concrete techniques available for making that tradeoff deliberately rather than by default. For a company running reasoning models at production scale, routing mechanisms that only send genuinely hard queries into expensive extended reasoning, while answering easy ones cheaply, is presented as one of the most immediately practical levers, directly affecting inference cost per query at volume. The authors' own caution matters for governance too, techniques that hide reasoning inside internal hidden states save cost but reduce what a human reviewer can actually audit afterward, so a compliance sensitive deployment may need the more expensive, visible reasoning approach instead of the cheaper opaque one right now.
explain_practitioner: Liu and colleagues systematize efficiency techniques for large reasoning models into two categories, explicit compact chain of thought methods, which preserve a human readable reasoning trace but reduce its token count through techniques like pruning redundant steps, and implicit latent methods, which encode the reasoning process inside the model's hidden states rather than generating it as visible output tokens at all, trading interpretability for speed. Beyond that core split, they catalog specific optimization techniques including model merging, architectural changes purpose built for efficient reasoning, and routing mechanisms that send easy queries to cheaper, non reasoning paths and only route hard queries into full extended reasoning. As a survey published in IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence and tracked in an accompanying public GitHub repository, its contribution is comparative organization of a fast moving literature, and the authors flag that the interpretability efficiency tradeoff, and the safety implications of compressing or hiding reasoning traces, remain open problems rather than solved ones.
